title: Moderation in eating
hookLine: a checkup, a lecture about salt, and a king who came to the Buddha puffing after a big meal
tomorrow: why would a Zen cook treat rice like his own eyes?

lines: A PRINTED SHEET AND A FROWN.
cards: Somebody comes home from a checkup with a printed sheet and a frown: less salt, less sugar, smaller plates. Advice like that usually lands as a scolding, and gets ignored by the weekend.
The suttas tell of a king who heard it differently. King Pasenadi of Kosala had eaten a big meal, the text says, and came to see the Buddha huffing and puffing.
The Buddha didn't lecture him, didn't list foods, didn't warn him about his heart. He spoke a short verse.

teach.b: The verse, in plain words: when a person is mindful and knows the right measure in eating, their discomforts grow fewer, they age more slowly, and they guard their life. That's all. No menu, no rules, no shame.
Now watch what the king does, because the story's real lesson is in the follow-through.
He asks a young man at court, Sudassana, to learn the verse and recite it to him at every meal. Each time the food arrives, the verse arrives too.
And the king, the sutta says, gradually ate less. Gradually is the key word. Not a crash diet by Friday.
Over time his body grew lighter, and one day, stroking his own limbs, he said the Buddha had shown him kindness in two ways: for this life, and for the next.
So here's what the tradition offers someone with a checkup sheet on the fridge. First, the measure is mindfulness, not hatred of the body. The verse begins with being mindful.
Second, the change is small and repeated: a little less, at each meal, remembered. Third, it helps to have a Sudassana, someone or something that brings the reminder to the table at the right moment.
A gentle line, said often, did what one stern warning couldn't. And the reward named in the verse is a life guarded, not a body punished.

how: Many Buddhist monastics eat at set times and keep meals simple; lay Buddhists often bring the idea of moderation home through a short reflection or pause before eating.

games.q: your dad wants to cut back on sweets after a checkup. what fits the Pasenadi story best?
o: throw out every sweet in the house tonight and start strict tomorrow.
a small cut, repeated, with a friendly reminder at the table.
say nothing; changing how someone eats isn't anyone else's business.
games.why: the king didn't crash; he had a verse said at every meal and gradually ate less.

practice: Think of your next meal and make a small plan. What would a little less look like there: one spoonful fewer, a smaller bowl, stopping at the first sign of enough?
Name what usually gets in the way, then choose one reminder, your own Sudassana, that could meet you at the table.

wordCard.voice: Moderation in eating: knowing the measure, mindfully, meal by meal, so the body is guarded and not punished, and the change has time to last.

orig.note: Pali: mattannuta, knowing the right measure, here in eating.

carryVoice: Here's the line: a little less, remembered at each meal. Eight of nine in the mind at home.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 3.13 (Donapaka Sutta: King Pasenadi, after a large meal, visits the Buddha huffing and puffing; the verse on moderation in eating; Sudassana recites it at each meal; the king gradually reduces his food)
